back: The smallest deployable unit -- one or more containers sharing a network namespace and, optionally, storage volumes.

front: Why not create bare Pods in production
back: A standalone Pod has no self-healing -- nothing recreates it if it dies. Use a Deployment instead.
You edit the Deployment (desired state, image, replicas, strategy); it manages a ReplicaSet underneath, which you almost never touch directly.
Rolls a Deployment back to its previous revision -- the fast fix for a bad rollout.
Pod IPs change every time a Pod is recreated. A Service gives a stable virtual IP/DNS name that load-balances across matching Pods.
A Service routes purely by label selector -- a mismatch between selector and Pod labels is a classic 'why can't I reach my app' bug.
ClusterIP: internal only. NodePort: static port on every node, mostly for testing. LoadBalancer: provisions an external cloud load balancer.
Partitions a cluster into virtual clusters for teams/environments/apps -- RBAC and quotas are commonly scoped per namespace.
No, not by default -- base64-encoded only, which is trivially reversible. Real encryption at rest needs to be set up deliberately.
Same injection mechanism (env vars or mounted files); the distinction is intent -- non-sensitive vs sensitive data.
Routes HTTP(S) traffic to many Services by hostname/path through one entry point -- does nothing without an Ingress Controller running.
Enforcement depends entirely on the cluster's CNI plugin -- some CNIs silently ignore NetworkPolicy objects.
PV = the actual storage resource. PVC = a request for storage that gets bound to a matching PV.
Enables dynamic provisioning: a PVC referencing it automatically creates a matching PV on demand, instead of an admin pre-creating one.
Role is namespace-scoped; ClusterRole applies cluster-wide (or to cluster-scoped resources like Nodes).
How a Pod authenticates to the API server as itself -- the workload-identity equivalent of an IAM role.
A templated bundle of manifests with configurable values.yaml, managed as one versioned 'release' via install/upgrade/rollback.
HPA scales the number of Pod replicas by metric. Cluster Autoscaler scales the number of nodes when Pods can't be scheduled.
Shows logs from the prior container instance -- essential right after a crash/restart, since the new instance's own logs are empty.

front: First troubleshooting command for a stuck Pod
back: kubectl describe pod <name> -- check the Events section at the bottom before anything else.
Hands-on performance tasks in a live cluster, no multiple choice. Passing score commonly cited as 66/100.
